title: The Image of the Invisible God
summary: Paul and Timothy greet the church at Colossae, thank God for their faith, love, and hope, and pray that they will be filled with the knowledge of God's will and live worthily of the Lord. Paul then sings of Christ as the image of the invisible God, the one through whom and for whom all things were made, the head of the church, and the one through whom God reconciled all things by the blood of his cross. He closes by describing his own sufferings and labor to make known the mystery of Christ among the Gentiles.
story: Colossians opens in the middle of the church's story rather than at its beginning. The Colossians had heard the gospel not from Paul but from Epaphras, one of their own, and it had borne fruit among them as it was doing all over the world. Paul, in prison, has heard about them and writes to a church he has never visited. This chapter lays the foundation for everything the letter will say: before he warns them about any teaching that would draw them away (chapter 2) or tells them how to live (chapters 3 and 4), he shows them who Christ is and what God has already done for them. The rescue from darkness into the kingdom of God's Son (verse 13) is the story of the exodus retold as the story of every believer.
historical:
Colossae was a small town in the Lycus River valley in the Roman province of Asia, in what is now western Turkey, near the larger cities of Laodicea and Hierapolis. Epaphras seems to have brought the gospel there during or after Paul's long stay in Ephesus in the mid-50s AD, when, according to Acts 19:10, the word of the Lord spread throughout the province of Asia. By the time of this letter Paul was a prisoner (4:3, 18), most likely in Rome around AD 60 to 62, though some scholars place the imprisonment in Ephesus or Caesarea; and some think a follower of Paul wrote the letter later in his name (see the introduction).

The church was mostly Gentile: the Colossians had once been alienated from God (verse 21), and Paul's gospel is the mystery now made known among the Gentiles (verse 27). The letter's warnings in chapter 2 show that some teaching was pressing on the church, apparently promising spiritual fullness through visions, rules, and attention to angels and spiritual powers. Chapter 1 does not yet name that threat, but its emphasis on Christ's supremacy over thrones, dominions, rulers, and authorities prepares the answer.
cultural:
Ancient letters began with the sender's name, the recipients, and a greeting, followed often by a thanksgiving or prayer for the recipients. Paul follows that form but fills it with the gospel: the greeting becomes grace and peace from God, and the thanksgiving becomes a summary of Christian life in faith, love, and hope. Letters were read aloud to the gathered church, which met in homes.

The people of the ancient world, Jews and Gentiles alike, believed the universe was full of unseen powers. Jewish writings of the period describe ranks of angels with titles like thrones and dominions, and pagan religion and magic sought protection from spirits and fate. The terms in verse 16 (thrones, dominions, rulers, authorities) name such powers, whether heavenly or earthly, good or hostile. Paul's point is that every one of them was created through Christ and for him. The language of inheritance and rescue from darkness also draws on Israel's history: Israel received an inheritance, a portion of the promised land allotted to each tribe, after God rescued them from Egypt.
literary: The chapter moves in four steps: greeting (verses 1 and 2), thanksgiving (verses 3 to 8), prayer (verses 9 to 14), and then the centerpiece, a passage many scholars regard as an early Christian hymn or poem (verses 15 to 20), followed by its application to the Colossians (verses 21 to 23) and a description of Paul's ministry (verses 24 to 29). The hymn has two stanzas that mirror each other. The first celebrates Christ in creation: he is the image of God, the firstborn over all creation, and all things were created through him and for him. The second celebrates Christ in the new creation: he is the beginning, the firstborn from among the dead, and through him God reconciles all things. The repeated all things, and the repetition of firstborn in each stanza, tie creation and redemption together. Some scholars think Paul adapted an existing hymn, adding phrases like the church and the blood of his cross; others think he composed it himself. Either way, it reflects how the earliest Christians worshiped.

outline.t: Thanksgiving for the gospel's fruit among the Colossians
Prayer for knowledge, fruitfulness, and thanks
The hymn to Christ, creator and reconciler
Reconciled, if you continue in the faith
Paul's sufferings and the mystery of Christ in you

doctrines.note: Christ is the image of the invisible God, the agent and goal of creation, the one who holds all things together, the head of the church, and the firstborn from the dead. All the fullness of God was pleased to dwell in him (verse 19). The church's confession of the full deity of Christ draws heavily on this passage.

All things, visible and invisible, in heaven and on earth, were created through Christ and for him, and in him all things hold together (verses 16 and 17). The creator of Genesis 1 is identified with the Son who became human.

God reconciled all things to himself through Christ, making peace through the blood of his cross (verse 20), and reconciled the Colossians by Christ's physical body through death (verse 22). Reconciliation assumes a broken relationship; the cross is God's own act to restore it.

words.note: Eikon, image. The word for a likeness or representation, like the emperor's portrait on a coin. It recalls Genesis 1:26-27, where humanity is made in God's image. Christ is the image of God in the fullest sense: in him the invisible God is made visible (compare John 1:18 and Hebrews 1:3).

Prototokos, firstborn. The word can mean born first in time, but in the Old Testament it also names rank: God calls Israel his firstborn son (Exodus 4:22) and promises to make the king his firstborn (Psalm 89:27). In the fourth century Arius and his followers used this verse to argue that the Son was the first created being. The church answered that firstborn here means supremacy and inheritance, and the next verse says all things were created through him, which excludes him from the things created.

Pleroma, fullness. The word for the full measure or complete content of something. Paul says all God's fullness was pleased to dwell in Christ (verse 19), and repeats the idea in 2:9. In later second-century Gnostic systems pleroma became a technical term for the realm of divine beings, but that usage came later; here it simply says that nothing of God is missing in Christ.

christ: This chapter is one of the highest points of the New Testament's teaching about who Christ is. He is the beloved Son into whose kingdom believers have been brought, in whom they have redemption and the forgiveness of sins (verses 13 and 14). He is “the image of the invisible God, the firstborn over all creation” (verse 15), through whom and for whom all things were made, and who holds the universe together. He is also the head of the church, the firstborn from among the dead, and the one through whom God reconciles all things by the blood of his cross. The same one who made the world has died and risen to remake it. Paul's own ministry is to proclaim the mystery long hidden and now revealed: Christ in you, the hope of glory (verse 27).

hard.q: What does Paul mean when he says he fills up in his flesh what is lacking in Christ's afflictions (verse 24)?
hard.a: Read quickly, verse 24 could seem to say that Christ's sufferings on the cross were not enough and that Paul must add to them. The rest of the chapter rules that out: reconciliation has already been accomplished through Christ's death (verses 20 to 22). Interpreters offer several explanations. Many connect the verse to the Jewish expectation of a set measure of suffering, sometimes called the messianic woes, that God's people must pass through before the end; Paul gladly takes a share of that measure so the church bears less. Others note that Christ is so united with his people that their sufferings are his (compare Acts 9:4, where the risen Jesus asks Saul why he is persecuting him), so Paul's sufferings for the church are part of Christ's afflictions in his body. Others read it as the sufferings required to carry the gospel to the nations, which Christ's work set in motion but did not complete. None of these readings suggests that the cross needs supplementing as a payment for sin; they concern Paul's share in the suffering that accompanies the gospel's spread.

questions: Paul's prayer (verses 9 to 12) asks for knowledge, a worthy life, strength, endurance, and thankfulness. How does that compare with the things you usually pray for?
If all things were created through Christ and for him, what difference does that make to how you view the natural world, or the powers people fear?
What does it mean to you that the hope of glory is Christ in you, rather than something you achieve?
